strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: real-time, streaming, long-horizon audio-driven avatar generation with high-capacity diffusion models. The system framing is compelling for ECCV because it targets a real deployment bottleneck rather than only improving offline sample quality.

The main technical components are well motivated. Timestep-forcing pipeline parallelism is a practical and effective systems contribution for turning few-step diffusion sampling into a high-throughput pipeline, and the same-timestep KV-cache design is clearly connected to both efficiency and training/inference alignment.

The rolling sink-frame mechanism, including adaptive attention sink and Rolling RoPE, directly targets long-horizon drift. The ablations show that history corruption and sink-frame handling materially improve long-video perceptual quality and identity consistency metrics.

Experimental coverage is broader than many avatar papers: the authors compare against several recent open-source methods, report perceptual, synchronization, identity, and runtime metrics, include long-video stress tests, provide an in-domain AVSpeech evaluation, and conduct a small user study.

The reported throughput is impressive: achieving about 20 FPS with a 14B model on 5 H800 GPUs is a meaningful engineering result, especially compared with the much slower diffusion baselines. The paper is also reasonably transparent about training scale, hardware, and some limitations such as time-to-first-frame latency.
weaknesses: The strongest claim, “real-time streaming,” is only partially supported. The method reaches real-time throughput after pipeline warm-up, but the reported time-to-first-frame is still 2.89 seconds, which is high for interactive avatar applications. The paper should more clearly distinguish throughput from interaction latency.

The quality gains are mixed. On GenBench-ShortVideo, the method is not consistently best in ASE, IQA, Sync-C, Sync-D, or Dino-S, and on AVSpeech it trails several baselines on FID, Sync-C, and Sync-D. The main advantage is the combination of acceptable quality and high throughput, not clear state-of-the-art visual or synchronization quality across settings.

The runtime comparison is not fully satisfying. Some baselines are run on a single GPU because their public implementations lack multi-GPU support, while the proposed system uses 5 H800 GPUs. This is practically relevant, but it makes the FPS table partly a comparison of available engineering effort and hardware utilization rather than only method capability.

The “infinite-length” evidence is suggestive but not definitive. The 10,000-second experiment repeats audio inputs and reports metrics on sampled 10-second windows; this may miss slow temporal artifacts, semantic repetition issues, or accumulated motion unnaturalness. The qualitative figures are low-resolution in the paper and cannot fully substantiate hour-scale stability.

Several components are adaptations or combinations of recent ideas: self-forcing/DMD, rolling KV caches, attention sinks, RoPE adjustment, and pipeline parallelism. The integration is valuable, but the algorithmic novelty beyond system co-design is moderate and should be presented with more precise attribution and comparison to closely related streaming diffusion systems.

Reproducibility is limited. Training requires roughly 500 GPU-days on H800s, the 14B model appears derived from WanS2V, GenBench is synthetic and not clearly released, and key deployment details such as communication overhead, memory footprint, quantization/precision, and failure cases are not fully documented.

The data and ethics discussion is too brief for a high-fidelity avatar-generation system. The claim that all identity data is collected with permission is vague given the use of AVSpeech, and the misuse discussion mentions access control and watermarking without evaluating or integrating safeguards.

strengths: The paper targets an important applied/systems problem: real-time, streaming, long-horizon audio-driven avatar generation with large diffusion models. I assess it mainly as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic one, which makes throughput, latency, robustness, and deployment evidence especially central.

The proposed system combines several sensible components: self-forcing/DMD-style distillation, timestep-aligned KV caching, pipeline parallelism over diffusion timesteps, VAE offloading, and a rolling sink-frame/RoPE mechanism for long-horizon stability. The overall design is coherent and plausibly useful for production-style avatar systems.

The runtime results are a clear positive point. The reported jump from roughly 4-5 FPS without TPP to 20.88 FPS with the full system, while using a 14B model, is practically meaningful if reproducible. The ablation in Table 3 supports the claim that both few-step distillation and timestep pipeline parallelism matter.

The paper includes several ablations and comparisons, including long-video ablations for AAS, Rolling RoPE, and History Corrupt, plus a small user study. The ethical discussion acknowledges consent, impersonation risk, access control, and watermarking.
weaknesses: The scientific case is not convincing enough for acceptance. Much of the technical novelty is incremental or system-integration oriented: DMD/self-forcing, causal KV-cache streaming, rolling attention/sink ideas, and pipeline parallelism are all closely related to prior work. The paper does not sharply isolate what is fundamentally new versus inherited from WanS2V, Self-Forcing, CausVid/LongLive, and other streaming diffusion systems.

The evidence for visual quality is weak relative to the claims. On GenBench-ShortVideo, the method is not best on ASE or IQA and trails OmniAvatar/WanS2V on synchronization metrics. On AV-Speech, it has worse FID than Ditto/OmniAvatar and worse Sync-C/Sync-D than OmniAvatar, yet the narrative emphasizes state-of-the-art performance. The main advantage is speed, not consistently superior quality.

The evaluation setup raises fairness and reproducibility concerns. GenBench is a newly created synthetic benchmark with only 100 short and 15 long samples, generated using proprietary or external generative models, and appears not to be public in the manuscript. The strongest claimed results therefore rest heavily on a private benchmark without enough detail to reproduce sample selection, prompts, audio generation, or evaluation protocol.

The long-horizon and 'infinite-length' claims are overstated. The 10,000-second experiment repeats approximately 10-minute audio and reports sparse metrics on short windows at 0, 100, 1000, and 10000 seconds. This does not demonstrate stable temporal coherence over the full duration, absence of accumulated artifacts, or robustness across diverse interactive conditions. Static frame snapshots and perceptual metrics are insufficient for such a strong claim.

The user study is under-specified and too small to carry much weight: 20 participants, no number of videos rated, no confidence intervals or significance tests, unclear randomization/blinding details, and unclear rating interface. The reported scores also do not clearly support the strongest claim, since WanS2V has higher synchronization and consistency than the proposed method.

The ablations are incomplete for an Applied/Systems paper. There is no detailed GPU utilization breakdown beyond a timeline figure, limited communication/memory analysis, no scaling study over number/type of GPUs, no robustness analysis under streaming audio arrival jitter, and TTFF remains high at 2.89s, which weakens the 'interactive real-time' framing.

Several comparisons are potentially unfair or unclear. Some baselines are run single-GPU because they lack official parallel scripts, while the proposed method uses 5 H800 GPUs. The FPS comparison therefore partly measures implementation/hardware parallelization rather than method quality. The paper should separate algorithmic generation speed, system throughput, latency, and hardware cost more carefully.

The writing and presentation have notable polish issues: table formatting is cramped, figures are hard to read, some claims are repetitive or imprecise, and terminology such as 'infinite-length' and 'only 5 H800 GPUs' is overstated. These issues do not alone determine the score, but they compound the reproducibility and clarity problems.

The method depends on a 14B proprietary-style base model, 500 GPU-days of training, and substantial hardware, but provides insufficient implementation detail for independent reproduction. The paper does not clearly state code/model/data release plans, licensing/consent details for AVSpeech preprocessing, or enough specifics for GenBench reconstruction.

strengths: The paper is best viewed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely new algorithm paper: its main value is the co-design of distillation, same-timestep KV caching, timestep-pipelined multi-GPU inference, and long-horizon stabilization for a large audio-driven avatar model. Under that lens, the contribution is significant and relevant to ECCV.

The Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism idea is practically compelling. The reported jump from roughly 4-5 FPS without TPP to 20.88 FPS on 5 H800 GPUs, while keeping a 14B diffusion backbone, is a strong systems result for real-time streaming generation.

The long-horizon consistency problem is well motivated, and the Rolling Sink Frame mechanism, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE, and history-corrupt training are coherent design choices. The ablations show clear gains for long-video perceptual quality and identity/semantic consistency, especially for History Corrupt and AAS.

The experimental section covers both short and long OOD generation, in-domain AVSpeech evaluation, runtime metrics, qualitative comparisons, and a user study. The results are not universally best on every metric, but they support the central claim: the method offers a strong speed-quality-long-context tradeoff compared with current baselines.

The manuscript includes useful implementation details, pseudocode, hardware configuration, runtime metric definitions, limitations, and an ethical discussion. These improve clarity and make the work easier to assess as a deployable system.
weaknesses: Several components are adaptations or combinations of recent ideas: WanS2V initialization/architecture, Self-Forcing/DMD, rolling KV caches, diffusion forcing, and pipeline-style execution. The paper’s originality is therefore more in integration and engineering than in a fundamentally new modeling principle; some claims of a new paradigm feel overstated.

The headline real-time result requires 5 H800 GPUs and about 500 GPU-days of training, which is substantial. Although the method is real-time in throughput, the reported time-to-first-frame remains around 2.89 seconds, limiting genuinely interactive use cases. The paper acknowledges this but the title and framing could better distinguish throughput from responsiveness.

The long-horizon and 'infinite-length' claims are only partially validated. The 10,000-second evaluation repeats audio to construct the test sequence and relies mainly on sampled windows and automatic perceptual/similarity metrics. This is useful evidence, but not fully convincing proof of stable arbitrary-duration generation across diverse real conversational scenarios.

The main OOD benchmark, GenBench, is custom and synthetically generated, with limited detail on prompts, selection criteria, possible filtering, and whether all baselines are equally advantaged by the benchmark construction. This makes the strongest generalization claims harder to independently verify.

The user study is helpful but small: 20 participants, limited protocol details, no confidence intervals or significance tests, and unclear sample counts per method. Some quantitative comparisons are also mixed: on GenBench-ShortVideo the method is not best in ASE/IQA/sync metrics, and on AVSpeech it trails some baselines on FID, Sync-C, and Sync-D.

Reproducibility is a concern. The system depends on a large pretrained model, large-scale compute, a processed AVSpeech subset, a synthetic benchmark, and detailed distributed inference implementation. The manuscript provides pseudocode, but without clear release commitments for code, model, data splits, and GenBench, independent verification would be difficult.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and significant applied/systems contribution: real-time, streaming, long-horizon audio-driven avatar generation with a 14B diffusion backbone. Treating it as an Applied/Systems paper is appropriate because the main value is the algorithm-system co-design rather than a single standalone modeling idea.

The technical design is coherent. The two-stage causal distillation, noisy history cache, adaptive sink, rolling RoPE, and timestep-forcing pipeline parallelism address concrete bottlenecks in streaming diffusion generation: train-test mismatch, long-horizon drift, flicker, and sequential denoising latency.

The empirical results are strong across several axes. On GenBench-Short and GenBench-Long, the method achieves much higher throughput than diffusion baselines while maintaining competitive or superior visual quality, synchronization, and identity consistency. The reported 45.2 FPS and 1.21s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs are impressive for a 14B model.

The ablations are useful and mostly well targeted. Tables isolating DMD, TPP, VAE parallelism, kernel optimizations, AAS, Rolling RoPE, History Corrupt, KV noise schedule, denoising steps, and block size make a credible case that the system gains do not come from a single hidden optimization.

The supplementary material improves the paper substantially: it includes in-domain AVSpeech evaluation with FID/FVD, a user study, 10,000-second stress tests, pseudocode, and implementation details for FP8, attention kernels, VAE caching, and multi-GPU scheduling.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with good motivation for why avatar generation is a special setting where static-scene priors and persistent identity anchors are reasonable.
weaknesses: The strongest claims, especially “infinite-length” generation and stability beyond 10,000 seconds, are not fully established. The 10,000-second evaluation samples short windows at a few timestamps and loops the audio from 7-minute GenBench clips; this is useful stress testing but does not prove arbitrary-duration stability under diverse, non-repeating interactions.

Reproducibility is a major concern. GenBench, evaluation scripts, and presumably important system code are only promised for camera-ready release. The method also depends on extensive engineering details, specific kernels, FP8 quantization, and 5-GPU H800 deployment, making independent verification difficult without code and infrastructure.

The benchmark is synthetic and small for long-video evaluation: GenBench-Long contains only 15 videos. While diverse synthetic prompts are useful, the paper would be stronger with larger real or semi-real long-form evaluation, more subjects, and clearer statistical variation across samples.

Baseline comparison fairness is imperfect. Some baselines are run single-GPU because official parallel scripts are unavailable, whereas the proposed method benefits from carefully engineered multi-GPU parallelism and custom kernels. This is acceptable for a systems paper, but the performance table mixes model capability, implementation maturity, and hardware utilization.

The long-horizon strategies rely heavily on a static-scene avatar prior. This is acknowledged, but it limits the scope: dynamic backgrounds, large pose changes, multi-person scenes, changing lighting, or interactive turn-taking may break the assumptions behind the sink frame and noisy history cache.

Some mechanistic explanations are plausible but not fully validated. For example, noisy KV as a low-pass filter and AAS as distribution-mismatch correction are supported by ablations, but the paper does not deeply analyze when these mechanisms fail or whether they introduce subtle loss of expression, motion diversity, or identity overfitting to the first generated latent.

The societal-impact discussion is brief relative to the capability being introduced. Real-time high-fidelity avatar generation has substantial impersonation and consent risks; the paper mentions access control and watermarking but does not evaluate safeguards or misuse resistance.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: real-time, streaming, long-horizon audio-driven avatar generation with large diffusion models. The combination of latency, quality, and long-form consistency is practically significant for telepresence and interactive avatars.

The system idea of assigning denoising timesteps to different GPUs (TPP) is a clear and potentially useful engineering contribution. The reported throughput gains over single-GPU and standard sequence-parallel inference are substantial.

The paper includes several ablations for the proposed long-horizon components (History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE), denoising step count, KV-cache noise scheduling, block size, and FP8 quantization, which helps isolate some of the claimed effects.
The authors discuss limitations and ethical concerns, including the static-scene assumption, real end-to-end latency, consent, and misuse risks.
weaknesses: The core scientific case is not convincing enough for acceptance. Many algorithmic components appear to be relatively incremental combinations or adaptations of recent ideas such as Self-Forcing, DMD-based distillation, rolling KV caches, noisy histories, and positional/RoPE adjustment. The paper often presents plausible intuition rather than deeper analysis or evidence that these mechanisms are necessary beyond the reported ablations.

The benchmark evidence is weak. GenBench is synthetic, small for long-video evaluation (15 long videos), generated with external generative models, and not released at submission time. This makes the main OOD claims difficult to verify and raises the possibility of benchmark bias or poor coverage of real-world avatar conditions.

The “infinite-length” claim is overstated. The main evidence for 10,000-second stability uses looped audio and evaluates short sampled windows at a few timestamps. This does not convincingly establish stable continuous generation over hours, nor does it test diverse long-form interactions, scene changes, accumulated semantic drift, or human-perceived temporal continuity.

The real-time/streaming claim is also somewhat overstated. The system requires 5 H800 GPUs for the headline 45 FPS result and the paper admits roughly 3 seconds end-to-end latency with network overhead, which is not sufficient for many bidirectional real-time interactions. The comparison to smaller or single-GPU baselines conflates algorithmic progress with much larger hardware budgets.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Some methods are run with different resolutions/crops or limited parallelization depending on official support; the paper compares a heavily optimized 14B model on multi-GPU hardware against methods with very different model sizes, deployment assumptions, and capabilities. Efficiency should be normalized more carefully by hardware, memory, cost, and latency.

The evaluation metrics are insufficient for the claims. ASE/IQA, Sync-C/Sync-D, and DINO similarity do not fully capture avatar naturalness, identity preservation over long time, motion realism, expression quality, or temporal artifacts. The user study is small (20 participants), lacks statistical significance analysis, and provides limited protocol detail.

Reproducibility is poor at submission time. The method depends on a 14B base model, 128 H800 training, extensive kernel-level optimizations, FP8, FlashAttention-3, cuDNN fused kernels, torch.compile, LoRA merging, and custom streaming VAE caching. GenBench and scripts are promised only for camera-ready, and many implementation choices are hard to reproduce independently.

Several claims are phrased too strongly relative to the evidence, including “model-agnostic and hardware-agnostic” TPP, “eliminate” drift/artifacts, and “infinite-length” generation. The limitations section acknowledges the static-scene prior but does not adequately address cases with dynamic backgrounds, multiple people, large head/body motion, changing lighting, occlusion, or interactive turn-taking.

The paper’s strongest results are primarily systems/engineering results, but the submission is framed partly as an algorithmic contribution. If assessed as an Applied/Systems paper, the hardware-dependent optimization and pipeline design are valuable, but the lack of reproducible artifacts, limited benchmark rigor, and overstated deployment claims remain major concerns.

strengths: The paper presents a compelling algorithm-system co-design contribution for real-time streaming audio-driven avatar generation with a large 14B diffusion backbone. I would assess it primarily as an Applied/Systems paper with algorithmic components rather than a purely Algorithms/General submission; under that lens, the throughput, latency, and long-horizon stability evidence are central and mostly convincing.

The technical ideas are well motivated and complementary: noisy KV caching/History Corrupt addresses error accumulation, Adaptive Attention Sink targets distribution drift, Rolling RoPE addresses conditioning/positional drift, and Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism maps the denoising process naturally onto multiple GPUs. The design is coherent rather than a loose collection of tricks.

The empirical results are strong. The method achieves 45.2 FPS and 1.21 s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs, while maintaining competitive or best visual quality, identity consistency, and synchronization on GenBench-ShortVideo, GenBench-LongVideo, and an AV-Speech held-out test set. The long-video ablations show clear contributions from the proposed stability mechanisms.

The paper includes meaningful ablations for efficiency, long-horizon components, denoising step count, KV-cache noise scheduling, motion-frame scaffolding, FP8 quantization, and block size. This makes the technical claims easier to trust than if only final comparisons were reported.

The 10,000-second stress test is unusual and valuable for this application domain. Even though it is not a complete proof of infinite-length generation, the segment-level metrics and qualitative examples provide useful evidence that the proposed mechanisms substantially reduce long-horizon drift.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with useful pseudocode and implementation details in the supplement. The limitations and ethical considerations acknowledge latency and misuse concerns, which are important for realistic deployment of avatar generation systems.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are somewhat overstated. “Infinite-length” is demonstrated through a 10,000-second rollout with looped audio and sampled segment evaluations, not through a principled guarantee or broad stress testing over diverse continuously evolving interactions. I would prefer the claim be framed as very long-horizon stable generation rather than infinite generation.

The evaluation benchmark GenBench is synthetic and promised for release only in the camera-ready version. Because the main out-of-domain results depend heavily on this new benchmark, reproducibility and independent verification are limited at review time.

Runtime comparisons are not fully normalized for hardware and resource use. The proposed method uses 5 H800 GPUs for its headline speed, while several baselines are run on a single GPU because their official code lacks parallel support. This is practically relevant, but the table can exaggerate the apparent FPS advantage without additional cost-normalized or per-GPU efficiency analysis.

The method is resource intensive: training uses 128 H800 GPUs and the main real-time configuration requires 5 high-end GPUs. This is acceptable for a systems-oriented contribution, but limits accessibility and makes reproduction difficult for most research groups.

Some metric choices are imperfect for the claims. Sync-C/Sync-D, Q-Align, and DINO similarity are useful but do not fully capture conversational naturalness, artifact accumulation, or identity preservation over hours. The user study helps, but details such as sample selection, statistical significance, and participant protocol are relatively light.

Several proposed mechanisms rely on a static-scene avatar prior. The paper acknowledges this, but the scope of validity remains narrower than the broad language sometimes suggests: large pose changes, dynamic backgrounds, multi-person scenes, and interactive bidirectional settings with lower latency are not convincingly covered.

The system combines many components, including distillation, FP8, FlashAttention, torch.compile, LoRA merging, VAE caching, VAE parallelism, and TPP. The ablations are helpful, but the overall engineering complexity may make it hard to isolate which gains are robust across different backbones or deployment environments.
